pulls.title: fuzz: torcontrol: drive the control connection over a mocked socket
pulls.body:
The `torcontrol` fuzz target hands made-up replies straight to the `TorController` callbacks, and caps each reply line at 16 characters. As a result:

- Most success paths can't be reached. They need lines such as `AUTH METHODS=...`, `ServiceID=<v3 id>` or `net/listeners/socks=...`.
- The code that parses bytes from the control port (`ProcessBuffer`, `ReceiveAndProcess`) and the command/reply chain are never fuzzed.

This PR adds:

- Allows reply lines up to 256 characters.
- Builds the values the fuzzer can't produce on its own:
  - v3 onion IDs, which need a checksum;
  - well-formed private keys;
  - `AUTH` lines that point at cookie files created for the test;
  - SAFECOOKIE server hashes.
- Drives a real `TorControlConnection` over a `DynSock`, with the harness playing Tor. This covers split writes, CRLF/LF line endings, async replies, EOF and reconnects. Direct handler calls are kept, so deep paths stay cheap to reach.
- Asserts that every command sent to Tor starts with a known command name and contains no stray line break.
- Keeps the target deterministic:
  - seeds the RNG;
  - clears `mapLocalHost` before each input;
  - only lets `COOKIEFILE` name files the harness created, so Tor input can't make the node read arbitrary host files.

The first commit fixes `DynSock::Wait()`. It wrapped `this` in an owning `shared_ptr`, so the socket deleted itself when the call returned. The bug has been there since #30205 and only showed up once this target called `Wait()`.

Coverage of `src/torcontrol.cpp`:

|        | lines | branches |
|--------|------:|---------:|
| master | 52.2% | 47.5% |
| this PR | 81.8% | 74.0% |

The master numbers come from the current qa-assets corpus. The numbers for this PR come from a short local run starting from the same seeds.

This changes the input format, so the qa-assets corpus for this target needs a refresh. I would be happy to open a a PR on qa-assets with new minimized corpus for this target.

pulls.title: policy: reject invalid CFeeRate values when deserializing
pulls.body:
**Problem:** With the `UnstableChain` IPC interface from #29409 merged, an IPC client could make `bitcoin-node` hit an `Assume` failure (debug builds) or compute wrong fees (release builds) by passing a malformed feerate to `broadcastTransaction`, `calculateIndividualBumpFees` or `calculateCombinedBumpFee`. These methods take feerates as serialized `Data` fields, and `CFeeRate` deserialization reads the fee and size without the checks its constructors do, so it accepts a negative size, which fee calculations require to be positive, and a zero size with a nonzero fee, which compares as an infinite feerate. Nothing deserializes a `CFeeRate` on master today.

**Solution:** Make `CFeeRate` deserialization throw on values its constructors cannot produce, the same way other malformed serialized data is rejected. The change is a `SER_READ` check in `src/policy/feerate.h` plus a unit test. It is similar to #36520, which handles other invalid arguments to `Chain` IPC methods.

This issue was found by Project Loupe and passed on by instagibbs.

pulls.title: net: stop monitoring select exceptions outside Windows
pulls.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
> 
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by ignoring the exceptionSet. Except on Windows, where we instead disconnect if its used.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

The PR makes two additional changes for clarity:
- wrap the `FD_ISSET` check in `#ifdef WIN32` (no behavior change)
- instead of `if (recvSet || errorSet)`, check `errorSet` separately and earlier (emits a different log message)

Test coverage is introduced in `p2p_socket_errors.py`.

Finally a similar fix is applied to HTTP.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization, while becoming very slow to deserialize.

This PR stores the stack as its serialization in a single allocation (or none if the stack is empty), with a small header holding its size and the offset of the last element. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place, only allowing replacing them entirely. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead. `CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes.

Later commits also introduce stricter checking during deserialization, rejecting the following before fully deserializing:
* Transactions with more inputs/outputs than are possible in a valid transaction.
* Transactions with 0 inputs or 0 outputs (applied in P2P, but not RPC etc. for backward compatibility).
* Transactions/blocks that exceed the 4M weight limit (also only applied in P2P).

The result is a significant reduction in the worst-case time and memory allocations needed for deserialization, both in valid and invalid transactions. With it, the worst-case memory of a valid deserialized block drops from 106.8 MiB to 6.0 MiB. Memory usage during deserialization can temporarily be higher: up to 7.8 MiB for valid blocks, and up to 13.4 MiB for invalid blocks, which can combine a few temporary vector allocations of up to 5 MB each.

Deserialization time and memory of the deserialized block, master → PR. Runtimes are medians in milliseconds. Memory usage is in MiB, and ✕ means rejected at deserialization time. Peak memory refers to the memory during deserialization itself, not persisted in the deserialized `CBlock` object. Numbers over 50 ms, 20 MiB usage, or 100 MiB peak are in **bold**.

| block | gcc | clang | mem | peak mem |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Valid blocks** |
| 1 tx, max 1-byte wit elems | **99.1** → 16.0 | **111.4** → 21.9 | **106.8** → 3.8 | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, max empty wit elems | **279.2** → 18.7 | **293.7** → 25.1 | **91.5** → 3.8 | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout, 1-item wit | 12.33 → 13.39 | 15.00 → 15.43 | 6.7 → 6.0 | 6.7 → 6.0 |
| max txs, 1 txin and 1 txout | 6.43 → 7.04 | 7.87 → 8.30 | 5.8 → 5.6 | 5.8 → 5.6 |
| 1 tx, max txins, 1-elem wit | 4.53 → 4.68 | 5.04 → 5.37 | 4.0 → 2.9 | 4.0 → 2.9 |
| mainnet block 969729 | 5.30 → 5.47 | 5.97 → 6.20 | 3.5 → 2.9 | 3.5 → 2.9 |
| **Invalid blocks** |
| 400k txs, many wit elems, truncated | **84.8** → 16.1 | **95.6** → 21.8 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 12.6 |
| 400k txs, big wit+scriptsig, truncated | **84.0** → 16.1 | **96.0** → 21.7 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 13.4 |
| 1 tx, 2M 1-byte wit elems | **98.0** → 10.6 | **109.9** → 16.2 | **106.8** → ✕ | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, 4M empty wit elems | **271.0** → 13.4 | **288.9** → 19.6 | **91.6** → ✕ | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max empty txs | **101.0** → 0.006 | **139.0** → 0.008 | **67.1** → ✕ | 67.1 → 4.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout | 27.6 → 7.3 | 34.5 → 8.5 | **23.4** → ✕ | 23.4 → 6.4 |

So in addition to improving worst cases very significantly, it also provides modest memory usage improvements to the common case. This translates to mildly increasing the effective capacity of memory-bounded data structures that store transactions, like the mempool.

Some notable changes:
* By implementing some checks (for inherently consensus-invalid things) in the deserialization logic, behavior may change. In particular, deserialization errors in P2P cause messages to be dropped/ignored, rather than triggering validation or net processing logic (which may include disconnections and/or inserting into reject filters).
* The rejection of transactions with too many inputs or outputs applies everywhere, including in RPC. That's hopefully a desirable change, but a change in behavior still.
* Random access to the witness stack elements becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$. This is not a problem for any validation logic, but may be relevant for the libbitcoinkernel API which exposes an individual element accessor.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

There are a few possible follow-ups:
* Enforce the 400k WU policy limit during transaction deserialization when active (instead of the 4M WU consensus limit).
* Extend this approach to entire `CTransaction`, allowing all transaction data to be stored packed together in a few allocations (rather than one per input, one per output, one per witness) plus some index structure to access it efficiently. That's a much bigger change, needing abstractions like #35569, but would reduce the maximum memory usage per WU for valid blocks from around 1.5 bytes/WU to 1.1 bytes/WU (compared to ~28 bytes/WU in master).

pulls.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pulls.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

pulls.title: streams: handle buffered write failures outside the destructor
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Block and undo writers buffer serialized data, then rely on the `BufferedWriter` destructor to write the remaining bytes.
`fwrite()` can report fewer bytes written than requested after a local storage error, e.g., if the filesystem fills up while a block is being written (my 1 TB benchmarking servers have recently been filling up, so I've been seeing these failures more often).
`AutoFile::write_buffer()` converts that result into an exception, and because the destructor is implicitly non-throwing, the exception invokes `std::terminate`.
Calling `flush()` before destruction is insufficient on its own because a failed flush leaves the same bytes pending, so the destructor retries the write while the original exception unwinds.

I introduced this bug in #31551 when adding `BufferedWriter`.

**Fix:** Block and undo writers now flush explicitly before destruction, catch write errors, log their cause, and request normal fatal shutdown, consistently with the adjacent file-close error handling.
`BufferedWriter` clears the pending byte count before writing, preventing a destructor retry after a failed flush.
The destructor uses `Assume` to detect missing explicit flushes before attempting a fallback flush.
`flush()` continues to propagate exceptions, and `AutoFile` remains unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Manual write-error reproducer</summary>

Force the error path in `AutoFile::write_buffer()`:

```sh
sed -i '' '/^.*AutoFile::write_buffer(/,/^}/s/!= src.size()/!= 0/' src/streams.cpp
cmake -B build && cmake --build build -j5 && build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"; echo "exit=$?"
```

Before this change, implicit flushing invokes `std::terminate`:

> libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::__1::ios_base::failure: AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
> zsh: abort      build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"
> exit=134

With this change, `bitcoind` logs the write failure and reports `Failed to write genesis block`, then completes normal shutdown and exits with status 1:

> Checking all blk files are present...
> [error] Failed to write block file FlatFilePos(nFile=0, nPos=8): AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
> ...
> Error: A fatal internal error occurred, see debug.log for details: Failed to write block.
> [error] Writing genesis block to disk failed
> [error] Error initializing block database
> ...
> Shutdown done
> exit=1
</details>

pulls.title: rpc: Report -rpcwhitelist denials as JSON-RPC errors
pulls.body:
This PR adds two JSON-RPC error codes for requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist`, which until now got an HTTP 403 status with an empty body:

- `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` (-38) is returned for a refused request, with HTTP 200 for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and 403 for legacy 1.x requests.
- `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` (-39) is returned for the other requests in a refused batch. A refused batch now gets HTTP 200 and an array with an error for each request, and still runs none of them.

**Problem:** `-rpcwhitelist` errors are currently handled differently from other JSON-RPC errors, so clients report them with vague or misleading messages, and for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests the handling does not follow [documented behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md#json-rpc-11-vs-20). Specifically, requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist` get HTTP 403 with an empty body, so the refusal shows up as a generic transport error rather than a specific JSON-RPC error. This is especially a problem for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, which are [supposed to](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/bf1a1f1662427fbf1a43bb951364eface469bdb7) report failed method calls only as JSON-RPC errors, not HTTP errors. The empty reply causes a concrete problem when JSON-RPC requests are sent over IPC instead of HTTP: `bitcoin-cli -ipcconnect` receives only the response body, so a refused call prints a JSON type error instead of a permission error, as described in a [private security review](https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/audits/ar-56/). Over HTTP, `bitcoin-cli` currently stops at the 403 status and prints only "server returned HTTP error 403" instead of the actual error.

**Solution:** Report whitelist denials like any other failed call: a JSON-RPC error in the body, with the HTTP status the request's version calls for. This brings the behavior in line with the documentation. `bitcoin-cli` then prints the permission error over both HTTP and IPC, with no change to the IPC interface. Small change to `src/httprpc.cpp` and `src/rpc/protocol.h`, with tests in `rpc_whitelist.py` and `interface_ipc_cli.py`. Details in the commit messages.

Compatibility: HTTP clients that send `"jsonrpc": "2.0"` or batches and check for a 403 status need to read the error code instead. Single 1.x requests keep the 403 status, now with an error body.

Open question for review: `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` could be named `RPC_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` is documented as batch-specific but would fit any request refused before it runs.

pulls.title: refactor: inline constant return values from `dbwrapper` write methods
pulls.body:
Related to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31144#discussion_r2223587480

### Summary
`WriteBatch` always returns `true` - the errors are handled by throwing `dbwrapper_error` instead.

### Context
This boolean return value of the `Write` methods is confusing because it's inconsistent with `CDBWrapper::Read`, which catches exceptions and returns a boolean to indicate success/failure. It's bad that `Read` returns and `Write` throws - but it's a lot worse that `Write` advertises a return value when it actually communicates errors through exceptions.

### Solution
This PR removes the constant return values from write methods and inlines `true` at their call sites. Many upstream methods had boolean return values only because they were propagating these constants - those have been cleaned up as well.

Methods that returned a constant `true` value that now return `void`:
- `CDBWrapper::WriteBatch`, `CDBWrapper::Write`, `CDBWrapper::Erase`
- `TxIndex::DB::WriteTxs`
- `BlockTreeDB::WriteReindexing`, `BlockTreeDB::WriteBatchSync`, `BlockTreeDB::WriteFlag`
- `BlockManager::WriteBlockIndexDB`

### Note
`CCoinsView::BatchWrite` (and transitively `CCoinsViewCache::Flush` & `CCoinsViewCache::Sync`) were intentionally not changed here. While all implementations return `true`, the base `CCoinsView::BatchWrite` returns `false`. Changing this would cause `coins_view` tests to fail with:
> terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::logic_error: Not all unspent flagged entries were cleared

We can fix that in a follow-up PR.

pulls.title: log: reduce excessive "rolling back/forward" messages during block replay
pulls.body:
### Summary
After an incomplete reindex the blocks will need to be replayed.
This results in excessive `Rolling back` and `Rolling forward` messages which quickly triggers the recently introduced log rate limiter.

Change the logging strategy to:
- Add single `LogInfo` messages showing the full range being replayed for both rollback and roll forward;
- Log progress at `LogInfo` level only every 10,000 blocks to track the long operations.

### Reproducer:
* Start a normal ibd, stop after some progress
* Do a reindex, stop before it finishes
* Restart the node normally without specifying the reindex parameter
It should start rolling the blocks forward.

Before this change the excessive logging would show:

pulls.title: guix: build glibc with `--enable-static-pie`
pulls.body:
From the glibc `2.27` release notes:

> Major new features:
> The GNU C Library can now be compiled with support for building static
> PIE executables (See --enable-static-pie in INSTALL).
> These static PIE executables are like static executables but can be

pulls.title: wallet: reject recipient amounts above MAX_MONEY
pulls.body:
`CreateTransaction` checks that recipient amounts aren't negative, but not that they're within `MAX_MONEY`. `CreateTransactionInternal` then sums them into `recipients_sum` (spend.cpp:1100) with no range check, and that sum can overflow.

Easiest way to hit it is `fundrawtransaction` with a raw tx that has two outputs of 2^62 sat. It can also be reached with only valid amounts through `walletcreatefundedpsbt`/`send`/`sendmany` and a few thousand 21M BTC outputs. The "Transaction too large" check only runs after coin selection, so it doesn't stop this. On master the node aborts:

```
Assertion failed: (!m_selected_inputs.empty()), function RecalculateWaste, file coinselection.cpp, line 904.
```

UBSan reports the overflow at spend.cpp:1100 first. With other values the sum wraps to a small positive number instead, and `fundrawtransaction` returns success for a tx with outputs of 46116860184 BTC each.

This checks every amount and the running sum against `MoneyRange` in the existing recipients loop of `CreateTransactionInternal`, before the amount is added to `recipients_sum`, and returns "Transaction output amount must be valid" before coin selection starts. The same check rejects negative amounts, so the separate negative check in `CreateTransaction` is removed. The new `test_outputs_above_max_money` in `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py` covers a single output above MAX_MONEY, two outputs whose sum is above it, a sum that overflows int64, and a negative output. On master the first case returns "Insufficient funds" and the overflow case crashes the node; with the fix all of them get the new error. `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py`, `wallet_send.py`, `wallet_basic.py` and `rpc_psbt.py` pass.

pulls.title: kernel: Dispatch log callbacks with btcsignals
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A kernel application whose log callback logs, or destroys a kernel object, hangs. The common way to hit this is a garbage-collected language binding: Python's garbage collector can run finalizers inside the callback, and a finalizer that destroys a chainstate manager flushes and logs (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34775#issuecomment-6278257737, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34374#discussion_r4030551866). The cause is that the kernel calls log callbacks while holding the logger's mutex, so any logging from inside a callback blocks on a mutex its own thread already holds. The problem is not new and has existed since logging callbacks were introduced in #30595.

**Solution:** This PR delivers log entries through `btcsignals::signal`, which calls callbacks without holding any lock, replacing the kernel's own callback list and custom dispatching mechanism.

The change is a usability improvement and a bugfix because with it applications no longer need to reason about deadlocks and blocking behavior from a mutex they can't see. However, they may need to be updated to deal with log callbacks that are no longer serialized and connection functions that no longer block. Compatibility details are in the commit message.

The main code change is in `src/kernel/bitcoinkernel.cpp` (+42/-77) accompanied by header docs and new test_kernel cases, which hang without the fix. There is also a commit switching `btcsignals.h` to use `StdMutex` instead of `Mutex` so it is safe to use in logging callbacks.

This is an alternative to the last commit of #34775, which fixes the same deadlock but only after limiting the process to one logging connection, and still hangs if a callback destroys the connection.

pulls.title: bip352: match P2SH-P2WPKH instead of evaluating it
pulls.body:
For P2SH inputs, `GetPubKeyFromInput` evaluated the full scriptSig with `EvalScript` and then ran `Solver` on the redeem script, even though only P2SH-P2WPKH is eligible for BIP-352. That costs time on every non-segwit P2SH spend (e.g. multisig), whose scriptSigs can be up to `MAX_SCRIPT_SIZE`.

BIP-141 requires the scriptSig of a P2SH-wrapped witness program to be exactly a single push of the redeem script (`SCRIPT_ERR_WITNESS_MALLEATED_P2SH`). So any valid P2SH-P2WPKH scriptSig is exactly `0x16 OP_0 0x14 <20-byte keyhash>`, and matching that template gives the same result without evaluating anything.

### Benchmarks

`bench_bitcoin -filter='BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_.*' -min-time=2000`, Release build.

Before:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|              688.30 |        1,452,858.07 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            7,158.19 |          139,700.11 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

After:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|               56.87 |       17,584,611.40 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            6,949.45 |          143,896.18 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

P2SH multisig is about 12x faster to rule out. P2SH-P2WPKH saves about 200 ns per input; its time is still dominated by `CPubKey::IsFullyValid()`.

pulls.title: crypto: copy HMAC state instead of rehashing key pads
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Setting up an encrypted connection derives six values with the same secret. Each HKDF expansion repeats two SHA256 compressions to hash the same HMAC key pads.

**Fix:** Hash the key pads once per HKDF context, then copy the prepared HMAC state for each expansion. The copy replaces two setup compressions, saving ten SHA256 compressions across the six outputs - the derived bytes stay identical. [RFC 2104 section 4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104.html#section-4) describes this optimization:

> the intermediate results … on the B-byte blocks (K XOR ipad) and (K XOR opad) can be precomputed only once

**Measurements:**

```text
BIP324_HKDF (ops/s, higher is better)
Before  █████████████████████████████████░░░░░░░  1,430,064  (baseline)
After   ████████████████████████████████████████  1,724,373  (+20.6%)
```

pulls.title: wallet, sqlite: Enable secure_delete by default
pulls.body:
Currently, when we make deletions or updates to the database that require records to be fully deleted and to not persist in free pages afterwards, we need to explicitly call `WalletDatabase::Rewrite`. This behavior was introduced in #635 to ensure that unencrypted private keys are erased from the database after encrypting a wallet, and initial encryption is the only consumer of this function.

However, initial encryption is not the only functionality that requires secure deletion. l0rinc's LLMs recently found changing the passphrase can leave the original that encryption key record in free pages. We should want to ensure that those records are also deleted, although I do not consider that the presence of such records in free space to actually be a problem. Note that this behavior appears to be present since wallet encryption was initially introduced in #352.

Fortunately, SQLite offers a secure_delete flag that can be enabled on each connection to a database. If set, all deletes or updates will ensure that any data that was deleted or overwritten actually are overwritten with 0's. It is one of the 2 methods in SQLite's documentation for ensuring that records do not persist in free pages, the other method being to call `VACUUM` after deletions or updates, which is what `Rewrite` does.

The downside is that secure_delete will increase CPU and disk I/O, which is why this was not set previously. However, it seems like several distros ship with secure_delete enabled by default: [Debian](https://sources.debian.org/src/sqlite3/3.54.1-2/debian/rules#L48#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), [Ubuntu](https://git.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/sqlite3/plain/debian/rules#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), [Fedora](https://src.fedoraproject.org/rpms/sqlite/raw/rawhide/f/sqlite.spec#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE=1), [Arch](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/archlinux/packaging/packages/sqlite/-/raw/main/PKGBUILD#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), and [NixOS](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/pkgs/development/libraries/sqlite/default.nix#L184) all set SQLite's compile time option to default secure_delete to enabled, and these are just the ones I've looked at. This suggests to me that the performance penalty is not actually that bad. As I run Arch and often do not use depends builds, I had not noticed that secure_delete was always on and did not experience any particularly poor wallet performance that could be attributed to that behavior. In the grand scheme of things, erases and updates are fairly infrequent in the wallet.

This PR enables secure_delete when the database is opened, and also enables it by default in the sqlite depends package. There are also a couple tests to check that all records we want deleted actually are being deleted from the database. `WalletDatabase::Rewrite` is removed as it it is no longer used.

pulls.title: validation: reduce per-transaction work
pulls.body:
Motivation: minor optimizations to slightly speed up validation by reducing resource usage.

I realize this touches consensus critical code and changes should not be made lightly. Open to feedback that the changes are not worth the performance gain, though I believe these changes can be made safely. To be specific:

1. Duplicate input check (CheckTransaction): replace the std::set with a pairwise scan for transactions up to 96 inputs. 2X to 3X speedup.
2. Relative lock times (EvaluateSequenceLocks): CalculateSequenceLocks returns {-1,-1} when no input has an active relative lock, so consult the previous block's median time past only when lockPair.second >= 0. Avoids an 11-entry walk plus sort for the large majority of transactions.
3. ConnectBlock: skip the per-input coin lookups that fill prevheights when BIP68 is not enforced for the block, the tx version is below 2, or every input sets SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME_DISABLE_FLAG. Correct because none of those cases can read a height.
4. Sigop cost (GetTransactionSigOpCost): fold the P2SH and witness counts into one pass over the inputs, halving coin cache lookups for P2SH txs.

I ran a few benchmarks / performance tests on this change. One set of benchmarks on my 8 core laptop solely for the duplicate input check change:

| inputs | old | new | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 9.61 ns | 7.65 ns | 1.26× |
| 2 | 20.09 ns | 9.12 ns | 2.20× |
| 2 (mixed idx) | 20.42 ns | 9.11 ns | 2.24× |
| 4 | 39.86 ns | 15.08 ns | 2.64× |
| 4 (mixed) | 39.29 ns | 15.03 ns | 2.61× |
| 8 | 79.50 ns | 30.70 ns | 2.59× |
| 16 | 248.71 ns | 79.39 ns | 3.13× |
| 32 | 577.75 ns | 224.12 ns | 2.58× |
| 64 | 1429.95 ns | 768.97 ns | 1.86× |

| 128 | 3208.11 ns | 3230.06 ns | 0.99× |
| 256 | 7682.29 ns | 7375.42 ns | 1.04× |

I also ran two sequential runs of `bitcoind --reindex-chainstate` on my 6 core desktop to try to compare before and after, the aggregate effect of all 4 changes.

pulls.title: rpc, wallet: Support BIP322 simple message signing
pulls.body:
## Description

The message RPCs currently support legacy compact signatures for P2PKH addresses. This adds [BIP322](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/a34f044bb8d5cd684d7a742d2f6483c14b719046/bip-0322.mediawiki) simple proofs for native P2WPKH, P2WSH and P2TR addresses, allowing users to sign and verify messages for these addresses without creating an on-chain transaction.

signmessage uses the wallet’s existing descriptor signing machinery and requires a complete satisfaction. This includes P2WSH multisig and supported Miniscript satisfactions, and Taproot key and script paths. It returns smp followed by the base64-encoded serialized witness stack.

verifymessage uses Core’s script interpreter to check the proof against the address and message. Verification requires no wallet or chain data and accepts both prefixed and older unprefixed simple proofs. Malformed base64 or witness serialization raises an RPC error; invalid proofs, unsupported signature formats and inconclusive results return false.

The RPC names and argument counts are unchanged. P2PKH compact signatures and signmessagewithprivkey retain their existing behavior. Full signatures, proofs of funds and P2SH addresses, including wrapped SegWit, are outside this change. Signing remains limited to satisfactions available to the wallet.

No consensus rules or signing-provider interfaces are changed. Help and release notes describe the supported formats and limitations.

Related earlier work: #24058.

## Tests

A shared fixture imports the applicable CC0 vectors from the pinned BIP: eight simple rows containing ten proofs, three hash cases and sixteen error cases. Published proofs are checked independently of locally generated signatures.

Coverage includes:

- bip322_tests and bip322_wallet_tests: transaction construction, parsing bounds, address binding, sighash and script rules, descriptor signing, incomplete satisfactions and wallet locking.
- rpc_bip322.py: published proofs in both encodings, invalid proofs and network-specific address parsing.
- Both existing message tests: legacy behavior, RPC errors and native witness signing.
- rpc_help.py: updated help.

The rationale for this PR is to improve the user experience in `new_db` failure to migrate a wallet.

#### My story

After using bitcoin core for a while -- and then ignoring it for a while -- I tried to open my old wallet with v31 release build, saw I had to migrate it, attempted to do so, and the app crashed; running from a terminal, I reproduced and got an error in the terminal:
```
./wallet/wallet.cpp:3868: bool wallet::CWallet::MigrateToSQLite(bilingual_str&): Assertion `new_db' failed.
```

### Explanation

Tracking down this assertion, I discovered the old BDB format was getting migrated to SQLite, but my wallet was stored on a CIFS mount (v3.1, `nounix`), which doesn't support the `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE` lock requested here. (`fcntl(3, F_SETLK, {F_WRLCK, start=1073741826, len=510}) = -1 EACCES`)

`MigrateToSQLite()` deletes the legacy BDB wallet before creating the new SQLite database, then asserts that the creation succeeded. Since this fails in my case (due to CIFS not supporting the requested lock), the wallet file is gone, leaving only the .legacy.bak copy made before migration. However, this could also be triggered locally by a full disk or permission errors.

This change attempts to populate the new database with a temporary filename, and only deletes the legacy wallet if that succeeds -- otherwise clean up the failed attempt and return an error with the underlying reason and a hint about filesystem locking. I included equivalent error handling/cleanup for other cases during migration that were also previously `assert`s, even though they weren't strictly part of the symptom I experienced.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create an old BDB wallet (e.g., Bitcoin Core v27) on a CIFS mount (definitely not the only way, but an easy path for me), or fill up the filesystem after creating the wallet.
2. Attempt to migrate the wallet with Bitcoin Core v31

Expected result: since the wallet cannot be migrated, the application should tell the user why and leave the original wallet in its original state.

Actual result: Bitcoin Core exits and leaves a 0-byte `wallet.dat` in its place.

### Tests

I added a few new tests covering this case and behavior change. I've only tested this on Linux. Without the fix, the tests abort on master.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Serving blocks to legacy nodes currently decodes and reserializes them just to remove witnesses. `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK` already avoids this work by serving the stored bytes directly. Faster witnessless IBD, as proposed in [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476), also needs peers to serve these blocks efficiently.

**Fix:** Read disk-backed, non-Signet `MSG_BLOCK` replies into an owned byte buffer, check the header's proof of work and expected hash, and strip witness ranges from that buffer in place.

Extract a shared helper so decoding transactions and skipping their bytes follow the same encoding rules. Signet keeps `ReadBlock` for its solution check. Header checks now precede transaction parsing, so records corrupted in both places can log a different error.

**Performance:**

Time to read a block from disk and build its non-witness message:

| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 1.31 ms | 0.147 ms | **8.9x** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 3.47 ms | 0.374 ms | **9.3x** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the raw witness-block serving added in [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151). The [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) and the closed [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098) identify unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. The implementation also builds on the bulk block reads introduced in [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551).

pulls.title: http: Restore requirement of IPv4 bind success
pulls.body:
### Problem

When bitcoind starts and the HTTP IPv4 listen address is occupied by another process, but the IPv6 address is available, the server fails open and generates a cookie file. When bitcoin-cli runs it picks up the cookie file and sends the credentials in plain text to the non-bitcoind process running on the default IPv4 port. An attacker can then use the credentials to commandeer bitcoind over IPv6.

### Solution

*Safe defaults*:
* When running with default settings, require that the IPv4 bind succeeds.
* When `-rpcbind` is specified, require that all HTTP listen socket binds succeed (fail closed-behavior).

Node operators who only have IPv6 are now required to override `-rpcbind` and `-rpcallowip` to only specify the working interface and allowed subnet if they were not doing so already.

The problem of bitcoin-cli sending the credentials to what could possibly be the wrong process remains **only in non-default setups**.

### History

40b556d3742a1f65d67e2d4c760d0b13fe8be5b7 from 2015 switched the HTTP server from Boost Asio to LibEvent, and binding switched from an attempt at dual-binding IPv4+v6 and falling back to IPv4-only (rpcserver.cpp / `StartRPCThreads()`), to binding IPv4 *or* IPv6 (httpserver.cpp / `HTTPBindAddresses()`). **The current PR restores the prior behavior of IPv4 being mandatory.**

#14968 from 2018 was an attempt to change the behavior to require *all* binds to succeed. But it ran into issues with poor IPv6 support on CI.

### Severity

This credential exfiltration attack requires capability to launch processes on the bitcoind host. If we are on the same account we can already read the cookie credentials off disk. So it's only really interesting when an attacker is on a different user account on the same host.

### Disclaimer

The first and last commits were probably initially generated with the help of silicon LLMs.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: replace `loadtxoutset` RPC with a startup arg
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Loading a UTXO snapshot through RPC requires coordinating with the active chain, mempool, caches and advertised services while the node is running.

**Fix:** Replace the `loadtxoutset` RPC with `-loadtxoutset=<file>` and finish importing during chainstate initialization, before networking and mempool loading begin.

pulls.title: i2p: pass base32 address directly to stream connect
pulls.body:
As the SAM protocol accepts a `.b32.i2p` address as the `DESTINATION` parameter for the `STREAM CONNECT` command, the `NAMING LOOKUP` round trip can be skipped on every outbound connection.

This should ostensibly make failure handling more accurate in certain situations as well, since a peer that cannot be resolved now returns `CANT_REACH_PEER`/`TIMEOUT` rather than there being an empty `VALUE=` key in the lookup reply. A missing `VALUE=` is a proxy error, so the attempt isn't recorded in AddrMan.

Router implementation versions that support this (Java I2P 0.9.48, i2pd 2.38.0) are older than ones supporting `i2cp.leaseSetEncType=6,4` (see #35696), so there should be no compatibility issues here.

Source:
https://i2p.net/en/docs/api/samv3/#sam-virtual-streams-connect

pulls.title: rpc: parse each batch element into its own request
pulls.body:
In a JSON-RPC batch, an element that is not an object gets an error reply with the id and version of the element before it.

`ExecuteHTTPRPC` parses every element of a batch into the same request object, and `parse()` throws on a non-object before it sets `id` and `m_json_version`. For `[{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"getblockcount","id":"X"}, 2]` the reply has two objects with `"id":"X"`, one with a result and one with an error. If the first element is a notification, the error is dropped. I give each element its own copy of the request, which holds only the HTTP fields, so the error is the one the first element of a batch already gets. The new case in `interface_rpc.py` fails on master and passes with this change.

pulls.title: rpc: handle malformed jsonrpc 2.0 requests correctly
pulls.body:
While reviewing #36642 I found something else we missed in JSON-RPC 2.0:

If we receive a malformed request we would assume that we couldn't parse it's jsonrpc version and send an HTTP error.  This is how the legacy jsonrpc server worked (despite that behavior not ever being part of any ratified jsonrpc spec) and we maintain it as Bitcoin "legacy" jsonrpc protocol. However it's possible to form a request that does properly indicate jsonrpc 2.0 but is still malformed. In that case, we should not send an HTTP error: the correct protocol is to respond with `HTTP 200 OK` and include the jsonrpc error message in the response.

The solution is to check if we know the request's jsonrpc version before responding with an error.

We already correctly handle such malformed requests in batches and this is already tested in `test_batch_requests()` in `interface_rpc.py`

On master, the functional test in this PR actually crashes the node because the assumption is codified. Note that this crash requires:
1. RPC Authentication
2. A debug build

So this is not an urgent security fix, but a bug that might disrupt testing.

```
node0 stderr httprpc.cpp:46
    UniValue JSONErrorReply(UniValue, const JSONRPCRequest &, HTTPStatusCode &):
        'jreq.m_json_version != JSONRPCVersion::V2' check failed.
```


In release builds the node doesn't crash, but it returns HTTP 400 with a JSON-RPC 2.0 error body instead of HTTP 200.

pulls.title: test: SRD tie-break test
pulls.body:
I was researching coin selection when I came across this bug, so I thought I'd fix it

Pr #33223  adjusts  weight selection to keep the lighter coin when two coins have the same value, but the test has two mistakes, as confirmed in this [comment ](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36255#discussion_r4432516127)

1. It builds `mixed_weight_pool` but passes `utxo_pool` to `TestSRDSuccess`.
2. There is nothing enforcing coin eviction because the current max weight (`4 * 3 * 67` = 804 WU) fits any two coins (544 WU)

If you reverse #33223, it still passes, which means it misses the tie-break

### The fix
The test now uses `mixed_weight_pool and adds an extra light coin so that only two light coins can fit together and evicts a coin on every tie to pass.
Lowers the max weight to 536 WU; SRD now has to evict the heavier coin on every tie to succeed

This should show failed tests with [bitcoin#33223](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33223) reverted and pass on master.

pulls.title: refactor : Reorder CBlockIndex members to save 8 bytes
pulls.body:
It seems we can save 8 bytes per CBlockIndex instance by reordering one class member. Moving one 8-byte field seems to avoid losing 2x 4 bytes to structure padding on a 64-bit build (on a 32-bit build, there is no gain).

I could not exactly measure the runtime gain from just this (smaller than RAM usage variation between 2 launches), but I confirmed there was about as many instances of CBlockIndex as blocks in the chain (increasing CBlockIndex size by 320 bytes increases RAM usage by ~300MB), so saving 8 bytes per instance should save about 8MB of RAM at current block height.

The gain is small, but it seems like it has no cost/risk, since that structure is not used for serialization, and just reordering here should have no side effects.

I saw a few other types that could gain a few bytes in size by doing something similar (for example, CTxIn), but they have far fewer instances in memory to make the change worth it.

pulls.title: net: reject oversized outbound messages
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Outbound transports encode message types in a fixed 12-byte field, but `CConnman` did not ensure internal callers respected this limit before queuing messages.
An oversized type aborts V1 encoding. V2 sends it under a truncated type with its payload intact, or writes past its encoding buffer when the payload is shorter than the excess type bytes.
The send path also did not enforce the 4 MB payload limit.

**Fix:** Treat oversized types and payloads as failed assumptions in `CConnman::PushMessage()` before they enter the send queue.

pulls.title: refactor: Add util::Result failure types and ability to merge result values
pulls.body:
Add `util::Result` support for returning more error information and make use of it in [LoadChainstate method](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25665/commits/b1c0feb6656befc48a6840c1d841074bd6131b78) as an initial application. Followup PRs [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) and [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) use it more broadly to return errors and warnings from wallet and kernel functions as well.

This change adds two major features to the result class:

- For better error handling, adds the ability to return a value on failure, not just a value on success. This is a key missing feature that makes the result class not useful for functions like `LoadChainstate()` which produce different errors that need to be handled differently [^1].

[^1]: Ability to return error values was actually present in the original implementation of [#25218](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25218), but unfortunately removed in later iterations. See [design notes](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/bitcoin-devwiki/wiki/util::Result-design-notes).

- For better error reporting, adds the ability to return warning messages and multiple errors, not just a single error string. This provides a way for functions to report errors and warnings in a standard way, and simplifies interfaces:

    ```diff
    -virtual std::unique_ptr<Wallet> loadWallet(const std::string& name, bilingual_str& error, std::vector<bilingual_str>& warnings) = 0;
    +virtual util::Result<std::unique_ptr<Wallet>> loadWallet(const std::string& name) = 0;
    ```

    ```diff
    -std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options, DatabaseStatus& status, bilingual_str& error);
    +util::Result<std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase>, DatabaseError> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options);
   ```

This change also makes some more minor improvements:

- Smaller type size. `util::Result<int>` is 16 bytes, and `util::Result<void>` is 8 bytes. Previously both were 72 bytes.

- Broader type compatibility. Supports noncopyable and nonmovable success and error types.

### Comparison with `std::expected`

Currently, the `util::Result` class is useful for error reporting—returning translated, user-facing error strings—but not as useful for error handling, where callers need structured failure information to decide how to proceed. By contrast, `std::expected` / `util::Expected` (#34005, #34006) is good for error handling but less helpful for reporting. This PR closes the gap between the two classes.

With this PR, `std::expected` remains a good choice for lower-level functions or simple functions that fail in only a few well-defined ways. Meanwhile,

- `Result` becomes a better choice for operations that can fail in many different ways—loading a wallet, connecting a block, etc.—where callers may want complete error traces, not just low-level errors without context or high-level errors without detail. (Followup [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) applies this to wallet-loading functions.) 
- `Result` can also be more useful than `expected` when merging status information from multiple calls. (Followup [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) uses this to reliably propagate flush and fatal-error status from validation code that can internally trigger flushes or shutdowns.)
- `Result` may also be a better choice than `std::expected` when returning pointer values. (Followup [#26022](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022) adds a `ResultPtr` specialization that avoids double dereferencing.) 
- `Result` can be more efficient than `std::expected` when failures are rare but failure objects are large, since failure values are heap-allocated.

This PR effectively makes `Result` a superset of `expected`, making the representations compatible and allowing them to be used together.

pulls.title: Add util::ResultPtr class
pulls.body:
<!-- begin based-on -->
**This is based on #25665.** The non-base commits are:

- [`3d008913cdb` Add util::ResultPtr class](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/3d008913cdb697651e67cd5ee158cc12a9611c0e)
- [`2d0915656c8` Use ResultPtr<unique_ptr> instead of Result<unique_ptr>](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/2d0915656c80d45642965b1963f158d865846f5b)<!-- end -->

---

The `util::ResultPtr` class is a wrapper for `util::Result` providing syntax sugar to make it less awkward to use with returned pointers. Instead of needing to be deferenced twice with `**result` or `(*result)->member`, it only needs to be dereferenced once with `*result` or `result->member`. Also when it is used in a boolean context, instead of evaluating to true when there is no error and the pointer is null, it evaluates to false so it is straightforward to determine whether the result points to something.

This PR is only partial a solution to #26004 because while it makes it easier to check for null pointer values, it does not make it impossible to return a null pointer value inside a successful result. It would be possible to enforce that successful results always contain non-null pointers by using a `not_null` type (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/24423) in combination with `ResultPtr`, though.

pulls.title: wallet: Track no-longer-spendable TXOs separately
pulls.body:
In #27286, the wallet keeps track of all of its transaction outputs, even if they are already spent or are otherwise unspendable. This TXO set is iterated for balance checking and coin selection preparation, which can still be slow for wallets that have had a lot of activity. This PR aims to improve the performance of such wallets by moving UTXOs that are definitely no longer spendable to a different map in the wallet so that far fewer TXOs need to be iterated for the aforementioned functions.

Unspendable TXOs (not to be confused with Unspent TXOs) are those which have a spending transaction that has been confirmed, or are no longer valid due to reorgs. TXOs that are spent in unconfirmed transactions remain in the primary TXO set, and are filtered out of balance and coin selection as before.

pulls.title: mempool: recalculate stale BIP68 lockpoints in removeForReorg
pulls.body:
When a reorg lowers the tip, `removeForReorg` can evict BIP68 transactions that are still valid at the new tip, together with all their descendants.

A transaction that spends an unconfirmed parent gets its lockpoints cached with that input at height tip+1. After `invalidateblock`, `TestLockPointValidity` can still pass on those cached lockpoints (always when every input was unconfirmed, since `maxInputBlock` is then genesis; and with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs when the confirmed input's block survives), so `CheckSequenceLocksAtTip` is evaluated against stale values and the transaction is removed.

The fix, suggested by ismaelsadeeq, is to never evict on cached lockpoints alone: if they are not valid at the new tip, or the cached sequence-lock check fails, recalculate them with `CalculateLockPointsAtTip` and evict only if the fresh result also fails. This covers height-based and time-based locks alike, at the cost of some recalculations that turn out to be unnecessary.

test_reorg_stale_lockpoints() in feature_bip68_sequence.py covers four cases across a reorg: a BIP68-disabled child, a BIP68-enabled child of an unconfirmed parent, a child with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs, and a time-based zero lock where the reorg lowers the median time past (test by Bicaru20). The test fails on master, and the mixed-input case also fails on the earlier genesis-only version of this fix.

test_reorg_unsatisfied_lock_evicted() (by instagibbs) is the counterpart: it checks that transactions whose relative lock is genuinely unsatisfied after the reorg are still evicted, together with their descendants.

Reproducer for unpatched nodes:
https://gist.github.com/javierpmateos/c55d365973adbf488a852dc5e0b77dec

Same class of issue fixed for TRUC in #33504.

Closes #35007

pulls.title: ipc: Expose Chain interface to IPC clients
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Processes connected to `bitcoin-node` over IPC (with `-ipcbind`) can use the `Mining` interface, but they can't currently use the `Chain` interface to read chain data or follow chain events. Chain data could be useful to third-party clients and Bitcoin Core's own wallet could use this as well to run in a separate process (#10102). But exposing all of `interfaces::Chain` to external clients would make its methods hard to change, since the wallet uses them as internal API (#34981).

**Solution:** Add capnp wrappers for `interfaces::Chain`, split into two interfaces backed by the same C++ class:

- `Chain`, returned by `Init.makeChain`, is stable. It follows Cap'n Proto schema evolution rules, so existing clients keep working as methods are added. It starts with the five block lookup methods: `findBlock`, `findFirstBlockWithTimeAndHeight`, `findAncestorByHeight`, `findAncestorByHash` and `findCommonAncestor`.
- `UnstableChain`, returned by `Init.makeUnstableChain`, extends `Chain` with every other method, for Bitcoin Core's internal C++ callers, such as the wallet, communicating over IPC. It can change in any way between releases. Incompatible changes renumber `makeUnstableChain`, so old clients get an error instead of calling the wrong methods.

Methods can move from `UnstableChain` to `Chain` once we're willing to support them for external use. `test/functional/interface_ipc.py` shows a Python client calling both interfaces. Like the existing IPC interfaces, these are only available to processes that can connect to the IPC socket, which already grants full node access through `Init.makeRpc`.

**Merge order:** This depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#377 and a subtree update that includes it (this PR currently carries that subtree change as its first commit), and on #36520, which fixes node crashes IPC clients could trigger with invalid `Chain` arguments.

---

This PR is part of the [process separation project](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/28722).

pulls.body:
Because the data directory may be a symlink, also log the path it resolves to, so `debug.log` files show the actual location for that run.

This patch would mostly help developers. I've been testing a potential performance PR across different data directories (for example, SSD versus HDD). After each run, I save the `debug.log` file. It would be nice if the `debug.log` file showed which data directory was used for that run.

It's easy to change the default directory to be a symlink. But in that case, `debug.log` doesn't show the actual data directory location. This patch changes the existing startup log line to show the resolved data directory path (after following symlinks) if it differs from the nominal path.

I don't think we need a separate test. I haven't tested on all platforms, but this patch uses primitives already used elsewhere, so it should work everywhere.

Here's an example of the changed line during startup (omitting the timestamp prefix):
```diff
- Using data directory /home/larry/.bitcoin
+ Using data directory /home/larry/.bitcoin (/sd/.bitcoin)
```

pulls.title: http: disconnect clients that never finish a request
pulls.body:
The -rpcservertimeout timer only measures inactivity. Every read from a client resets it, so a client that keeps sending bytes without ever completing a request can hold the connection for ever. 

Connection slots are capped by default 16 or by -rpcmaxconnections. Once those slots are taken, the server stops accepting new connections. Because no request ever completes the authentication functions are never hit. 
The impact is low because RPC port binds to localhost by default, so this is a robustness fix rather than a remotely exploitable security issue.

<details> <summary> How to reproduce </summary>

To reproduce: start a node with -rpcmaxconnections=2, open two sockets, and write "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n" one byte at a time with ten seconds between bytes. bitcoin-cli getblockcount then hangs until one of the (trickling) sockets is closed.

</details>

The fix adds a second deadline next to the idle timer. It is armed on the first byte of a request and expires after -rpcservertimeout (the same value as the idle timer). This timer also does not resets or is extended by later reads. Completing request parsing clears the deadline, so a long-running RPC keeps its connection as before. The deadline is deferred while a worker holds the request, for the same reason the idle timer is. It is restarted while response bytes
are written, because the client cannot start a new request during that window. -rpcservertimeout=0 disables both timers. No new option is added.

Disclaimer this bug is found by utilizing ASTRA. Verified using KIMI 3 and Claude.

pulls.title: qa: assert_equals -> assert_true/assert_false
pulls.body:
Instead of this in the functional tests:
```python
    assert_equals([long expression pushing next arg to the right], True)
    assert_equals([other long expression pushing next arg to the right], False)
```
we get:
```python
    assert_true([long expression without arg on the right side..])
    assert_false([other long expression without next arg to the right.])
```

The main point of this change is that `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` reduce cognitive tokens when scanning the code (equals to *what*...?). (As a consequence, `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` are also common in other test frameworks).

`assert_equals()` continues to be used in cases where we don't compare to boolean literals.

`assert_true([expression])` is different from plain `assert [expression]` in that `assert` is truthy while `assert_true` requires boolean `True`. (`assert` can also be deactivated when executing Python code in optimized mode (see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30529#discussion_r1893029530)).

A smaller scale attempt at introducing `assert_true()` was originally included in #31874 before being dropped.

pulls.title: scripted-diff: Type-safe settings retrieval
pulls.body:
This PR changes the way settings are registered and retrieved to provide more compile-time safety. Currently settings are [registered](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/03cff2c1421e5db59963eba1a845ef5dd318c275/src/init.cpp#L504) and [retrieved](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/03cff2c1421e5db59963eba1a845ef5dd318c275/src/init.cpp#L173) like:

```c++
// Register setting
argsman.AddArg("-pid=<file>", strprintf("Specify pid file. Relative paths will be prefixed by a net-specific datadir location. (default: %s)", BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME), ArgsManager::ALLOW_ANY, OptionsCategory::OPTIONS);

// Retrieve setting
args.GetPathArg("-pid", BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME)
```

But this is not ideal because nothing checks that setting names are spelled correctly, or that default values (`BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME`) are used consistently in the help string and retrieval sites, or that settings are retrieved with consistent types (bool, int, string, path, or list). This PR addresses these issues by adding setting [declarations](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init_settings.h#L267-L270) which allow settings to be [registered](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init.cpp#L484) and [retrieved](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init.cpp#L164C38-L164C59) like:

```c++
// Declare setting
using PidSetting = common::Setting<
    "-pid=<file>", fs::path, {.legacy = true},
    "Specify pid file. Relative paths will be prefixed by a net-specific datadir location. (default: %s)">
    ::DefaultFn<[] { return BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME; }>;

// Register setting
PidSetting::Register(argsman);

// Retrieve setting
PidSetting::Get(args)
```

---

#### Suggestions for review

All the real changes in this PR are in the last scripted-diff commit:

- [scripted-diff: Replace AddArgs / GetArgs calls with Setting Register / Get calls](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31260/commits/73c1f852eba2a48be0f03816a957e46ce6275bd9)

If you take a few minutes to look at the changes applied in this scripted-diff commit, you'll understand everything this PR is doing. A good place to start looking around in this commit is the generated [`src/init_settings.h`](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/pr/scripty/src/init_settings.h) file which declares the settings that get registered in [src/init.cpp](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/pr/scripty/src/init.cpp). Then you can look at the surrounding diffs and see they are just replacing `AddArg` and `GetArg` calls.

The other notable commit is second commit, which implements the `Setting` class:

- [common: Add Setting class to support typed Settings](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31260/commits/9c1cdb31eac5a180950dee0c6135918ce70b60f1)

The other commits do minor things like moving code or updating linters. The python script that implements the scripted diff is a temporary artifact that gets deleted. The python script is complicated because it does things like parsing c++ code to extract help strings, and figuring out the right types to declare settings with so code compiles. But the entire scope of the script is to (1) generate Setting type definitions, (2) add #includes, and (3) replace `AddArg()` calls with `Register()` calls and `GetArg()` calls with `Get()` calls. So there is not much the script can actually do wrong without triggering build and test failures.

---

#### Extensions

This PR only adds the ability to declare individual settings with built-in types. It doesn't provide any new runtime behavior, but a branch in issue #22978 extends the `Setting` class implemented here to support runtime setting validation, additional types like `std::variant`, additional conversion options, custom types, custom validation, and groups of settings declared as options structs.

This change is mostly orthogonal to #16545. #16545 only provides runtime type checking while this PR only provides compile-time checking with no new runtime behavior. But this change does allow a nicer way of declaring types in #16545, using c++ types like `int` instead of flags like `ALLOW_INT`, or`std::vector<std::string>` instead of `ALLOW_STRING | ALLOW_LIST`.

Split out of #36608, the overall private broadcast rework to support ease of review for like-for-like feature.

Differences from #36608 :
1. No tool support or prep refactors for the tool
2. No package relay
3. Slimmed down test profile focusing on protecting aginst IP address linkage and not crashing the node on adversarial inputs (which is a leak in itself)

With `-privatebroadcast`, `sendrawtransaction` queues a job instead of handing the transaction to

pulls.title: test: allow 3 bytes of fee overestimate in assert_fee_amount
pulls.body:
The wallet sizes a transaction assuming a 71-byte low-R ECDSA signature. A signature whose r or s has leading zero bytes is shorter, so the fee can cover a few bytes more than the signed transaction needs. In #36394 the wallet estimated 219 bytes and paid 438 sat at 2 sat/vB, but the signed transaction was 216 bytes: the signature was 3 bytes short. That happens about once in 4 million signatures. `assert_fee_amount` allows only 2 bytes of overestimate, so the test failed.

I raise the allowance to 3 bytes, which makes the failure about 200 times rarer. The check that the fee is not too low is unchanged. @maflcko suggested 3 bytes in #24151 and #25164.

Fixes #36394.

pulls.title: wallet: allow skipping script paths
pulls.body:
While testing MuSig2 integration in #29675 I ran into a Ledger bug https://github.com/LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin-new/issues/329 that was triggered because we signed for a script path in addition to the key path. The bug itself will be fixed, but it seems useful in general to be able to skip script path signing (and finalizing).

For example, you may have a 2-of-2 musig() descriptor with some sort of fallback after coins are N blocks old. For both on chain privacy and fee reasons, you don't want to use this path unless absolutely necessary. But our wallet can't know if our co-signer still has their key, so we sign the script path at all times. This could lead to accidental broadcast.

This PR introduces a `keypath_only` option (default `false` for now) to the following RPC methods:
- `send` 
- `sendall`
- `walletcreatefundedpsbt`
- `walletprocesspsbt`
- `descriptorprocesspsbt`

The resulting PSBT won't _add_ `taproot_scripts` or `taproot_script_path_sigs`. It does still have `taproot_bip32_derivs` and `musig2_participant_pubkeys`.

It will not remove `taproot_scripts` from an existing PSBT, but it won't add a corresponding entry to `taproot_script_path_sigs`. We also won't finalize a PSBT without keypath spend, even with complete script paths. This protects against other participants accidentally including them.

The `wallet_taproot.py` tests are expanded to cover this behavior.

It can also be tested with https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

pulls.title: validation: Avoid rewriting genesis block when already on disk
pulls.body:
fixes #33128

this picks up #33164

on a normal start (without `-reindex`), `CompleteChainstateInitialization()`
calls `LoadGenesisBlock()`, which writes the genesis block to `blk00000.dat`
unless the block index already contains it. if `blocks/index` was deleted,
then the index is empty, so genesis is _unconditionally_ written again
even though the file is still intact on disk and holds all the later blocks

that write eventually reaches `AllocateFileRange()`, which allocates
space from the start of the file. with `posix_fallocate()`, this only
reserves space. on platforms without it (e.g. OpenBSD, NetBSD), the
fallback writes zeroes over the requested range, replacing the blocks
that were already there

only after that, does the node notice that the chainstate no longer
matches the block index and fail with `"Error initializing block database"`,
asking for `-reindex`. by then, the blocks are already gone, so the reindex
finds the genesis only, reports success, and `getblockcount` returns `0`

---

this PR makes `LoadGenesisBlock()` read the genesis block back _from
disk first_ and only write it when it is not already there. if genesis
is already on disk, update the blockfile info with its position and
size so that the next block is written after it instead of overwriting it

pulls.title: wallet: relax external_signer flag constraints
pulls.body:
The `external_signer` indicates that an external signer device may be called via [HWI](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/HWI) or [equivalent](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/external-signer.md#signer-api) application.

When it was initially introduced some additional constraints were placed on wallets with this flag: it had to be a descriptor wallet and watch-only. Also the flag could not be added or removed later.

The constraints aren't a problem for the main supported and documented use case of connecting a single hardware wallet and using it just like a normal single sig Bitcoin Core wallet.

But they get in the way of MuSig2 support, see https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

This pull request drops the following constraints:

- `disable_private_keys` is no longer mandatory (but still default)
- `external_signer` flag is now mutable

Changing the `external_signer` flag reloads the wallet so that its descriptor ScriptPubKeyMans are recreated using the new setting.

Additionally it does the following:

- make the `blank` option for `createwallet` consistent with regular wallets by _not_ importing keys from the connected signer
- avoid going through `createTransaction` for external signers (otherwise the GUI breaks)
- create an `ExternalSignerScriptPubKeyMan` when importing a descriptor into an external signer wallet, instead of requiring an additional reload

This should have no noticeable effect on the default single sig use case described above.

Finally we add test coverage for spending from an imported hot key descriptor in an external signer wallet. The wallet signs with its own keys before involving the external signer.

pulls.title: Interfaces: Expose UTXO Snapshot Loading and Add Progress Notifications
pulls.body:
# Add UTXO Snapshot Loading Interface and Progress Notifications

This PR implements a complete interface for loading UTXO snapshots through the GUI, including progress notifications to provide user feedback during the loading process.

---

## Changes

### Commit 1: interfaces: expose UTXO snapshot functionality (loading/activate) in node interface

- Added a new virtual method `snapshot` to the node interface for loading UTXO snapshots from a path.
- Added `snapshot.h` to `src/interfaces` defining the Snapshot interface; `activate()` returns `util::Result<const CBlockIndex*>` to   carry either the base block index on success or a descriptive error message on failure, matching the shape of `ChainstateManager::ActivateSnapshot()`.
- Added a `getMetadata` accessor so callers can read snapshot metadata populated during activation without re-parsing the file.
- Added `SnapshotImpl` in src/node/interfaces.cpp: opens the snapshot file, parses metadata, and forwards to `ChainstateManager::ActivateSnapshot()`, propagating any error as util::Error{...}.

This change enhances the user's ability to load UTXO snapshots through the GUI and/or RPC.

### Commit 2: `notifications: Implement snapshot load progress notifications`

- Added a new signal `SnapshotLoadProgress` for snapshot load progress in the UI interface.
- Updated the notifications interface to include a method for reporting snapshot loading progress.
- Enhanced the `ChainstateManager` to report progress during snapshot loading.
- Implemented the necessary handler in the kernel notifications to relay progress updates.

This change improves user feedback during the snapshot loading process.

### Commit 3: `rpc: refactor loadtxoutset to use snapshot interface`

- Updated the `loadtxoutset` RPC to call the new snapshot interface instead of directly working with chainstate internals. File opening, metadata parsing, and activation now all happen inside `interfaces::Snapshot::activate()` rather than being split between the RPC handler and the interface.
- Removed the redundant pre-parse block in the RPC handler; its file-open and metadata-parse work duplicated what activate() already performs.
- Collapsed the RPC error handling to a single `RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR` built from `util::ErrorString(activation_result).original`, using the `"Unable to load UTXO snapshot: %s. (%s)"` format established in #30267 / #30395.
- Read `coins_loaded` from `snapshot->getMetadata()` after `activate()` populates it.
- Updated `feature_assumeutxo.py` to assert on the unified error code for file-open and metadata-parse failures (message substrings unchanged).
Improves modularity by consolidating snapshot handling through the interface layer.
---

## Technical Details

The implementation includes:

- **UI Interface Enhancement**
  Added `SnapshotLoadProgress` signal to `CClientUIInterface` with corresponding signal declaration and implementation.

- **Node Interface**
  Added `loadSnapshot` virtual method to the node interface with implementation in `interfaces.cpp`.

- **Progress Notifications**
  Implemented `snapshotLoadProgress` method in `KernelNotifications` class to relay progress updates to the UI.

- **Base Interface**
  Added `snapshotLoadProgress` virtual method to the kernel notifications interface.

---

## Benefits

- **User Experience**
  Provides real-time feedback during UTXO snapshot loading operations.

- **GUI Integration**
  Enables loading UTXO snapshots directly through the Bitcoin Core GUI.

- **Progress Tracking**
  Users can monitor the progress of snapshot loading operations.

- **Consistent Interface**
  Follows the existing pattern for progress notifications in the codebase.

## Testing

```bash
./bitcoin-cli -rpcclienttimeout=0 -signet loadtxoutset /path/to/utxo-snapsshot.dat
```
